titulo.texto: Chuj / Traditional Wool Overcoat from San Juan Chamula

frase_gancho.texto: Black wool, thick as felt, to keep warm in the mist of the Chiapas Highlands.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the wool of the Highlands, we move on to painting. Look for a small mural with a fantastical air, signed by Leonora Carrington, the painter who traveled to those same Chiapas Highlands.

guion_corto.texto: This black wool tunic, called a chuj in Tzotzil, is the garment worn by the men of San Juan Chamula, a town in the Chiapas Highlands, more than two thousand meters above sea level. It is a short, sleeveless tunic, with an opening for the head and others at the sides for the arms. The women shear the sheep, wash the wool, spin it with a spindle whorl, and weave it on a backstrap loom. The result is a cloth so thick and dense that it protects against the cold and the rain of the highlands. Notice the loose threads that hang down at the bottom and sway as the wearer walks. For the Chamulas, this garment is much more than a coat: it tells who you are and which community you belong to.

guion_largo.texto:
If you came down to see [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal), Chaac, and the [Queen of Uxmal](mna_s09_reina_uxmal), you may have been left with the idea that the Maya are a mystery of the past. This hall says the opposite. According to census data, more than two million people in Mexico speak a Maya language today, and our journey through them begins in the mountains, with the Tzotzil of the Chiapas Highlands.

San Juan Chamula is a town known for the strength of its customs. In its church there are no pews: the floor is covered with pine needles, families light hundreds of candles, and prayers are spoken in Tzotzil. The patron saint is Saint John the Baptist, who is depicted with a lamb, and it is said that this is where the respect for sheep comes from, since they are raised to be shorn and not to be eaten. Thus, every tunic is made from the wool of a respected animal.

There is a surprising fact: before the arrival of the Spaniards, there were no sheep in the Americas. The Maya wove cotton, which does not grow in cold lands, and wool arrived with the Europeans in the sixteenth century. The Tzotzil people took it up and made it so much their own that today it seems part of the landscape. What did not change was the backstrap loom, the same one that appears in some ancient images of the goddess Ixchel, whom we discussed in the Hall of the Indigenous Peoples.

When the cloth comes off the loom, it is loose and light. Then it is boiled and beaten so that the fibers tangle together and the wool turns into felt. This treatment is called fulling, and it is what gives the tunic its thickness. In addition, wool has a virtue that cotton does not: it keeps you warm even when it gets wet, something very valuable in a mountain region where winter dawns can bring frost.

Each Tzotzil town is recognized by its clothing, and within the town, clothing tells who you are. In many towns of the Highlands, serving the community is a post that rotates, almost always for one year and without pay, and whoever holds it wears its own insignia, such as ribbons, staffs, or a certain kind of tunic. It is said that the thickest and darkest ones belong to the traditional authorities, such as the stewards. As they pass by, everyone knows who holds the responsibility.

Notice also what is missing: there are no dyes. The colors of the wool, black, white, or dark brown, are those of the sheep itself. The garment, then, has the color of the things of the mountain: the shadows of the forest, the low clouds, the wet earth.

In this same hall there is another view of Chiapas: the great mural “El mundo mágico de los mayas,” by the Surrealist painter [Leonora Carrington](mna_s19_mural_carrington), from the early 1960s. She traveled to Chiapas and painted healers, animals, and sacred mountains based on stories from the region. It is not a photograph but a dream, and it is worth looking at slowly.

A single garment thus holds the work of women, respect for an animal, the authority of a community, and the pride of a language. As you continue through the hall, notice how many times that thread returns: making, caring, and sharing.

texto.Technique/Material: Black sheep’s wool, hand-spun and hand-woven, with yarn tassels
texto.Function: Men’s ceremonial garment, marker of rank in the cargo system, and mountain outerwear

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Maya disappeared centuries ago.
texto.respuesta: Reality: More than two million people in Mexico speak a Maya language today, and they dress, weave, and celebrate as their grandparents did.
